chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Is an Inflation Regime?

lessons.title: Demand-Pull, Cost-Push, and Monetary Inflation: The Three Engines

children.text: The last lesson established the core distinction: a headline CPI print is just a number, the regime behind it is the mechanism. Every inflation regime you will study in this course, from Weimar Germany's hyperinflation to India's post-COVID price surge, traces back to one of three engines. Learn to identify these three and you can read almost any inflation episode in history, including the one playing out in India right now.

body.text: Prices rise for one of three reasons: too much demand chasing too few goods, rising costs squeezing supply, or too much money chasing the same goods. Most real episodes blend two or three, but one engine almost always dominates, and identifying which one is the whole game.

A common mistake, encouraged by TV debates, is to blame every price rise on "greedy companies" raising prices, a cost-push story. Sometimes that is true. Often the real driver is a demand or monetary regime, and pinning it on corporate greed just delays the correct diagnosis, and the correct policy response.

children.text: Demand-pull inflation happens when spending power in the economy grows faster than the economy's ability to produce goods and services. More people have more money and credit to spend, so they bid up the price of the same fixed supply of homes, cars, and services. India's 2003-08 boom is the textbook domestic case: cheap credit, rapid GDP growth, and a young workforce entering high-paying IT and services jobs sent consumption and real estate demand soaring, and the

rallied nearly sixfold between 2003 and their January 2008 peak. By late 2007 and into 2008, that same demand boom, combined with a global commodity rally, was showing up as double-digit WPI inflation.

body.label: Classic Demand-Pull Signal
body.value: Core inflation rising alongside strong GDP growth
body.context: When both move up together, the economy is running hot, not being squeezed from the supply side.

children.text: Cost-push inflation happens when the cost of producing goods rises, for reasons that have nothing to do with demand, and businesses pass that cost onto the price tag. The 1973 and 1979 oil shocks, covered in the next chapter, are the global textbook cases: OPEC supply cuts sent crude prices up several-fold within months, and every economy that imported oil saw transport, manufacturing, and food costs rise together. India lived a recent version of this in 2021-22: global crude and edible oil prices spiked after the Russia-Ukraine war disrupted supply, and since India imports roughly 85% of its crude oil and a large share of its edible oil, the cost shock flowed straight through to diesel, LPG, and packaged food prices on grocery shelves across the country, from metro kirana stores to rural haats.

Monetary inflation happens when the money supply itself grows faster than the real economy can absorb, regardless of what any individual business or household is doing. This is the engine behind every genuine hyperinflation in history, including Weimar Germany's, which you will study in the next chapter. body.caption: Money supply (M) times velocity of money (V) equals price level (P) times real output (Q). Hold Q roughly fixed and grow M much faster than the economy can absorb, and P has to rise to balance the equation.

body.title: Why Monetary and Rate Moves Show Up Late: The RBI Transmission Lag

events.title: RBI Moves the Repo Rate
events.description: The Monetary Policy Committee cuts or hikes the repo rate. Markets react within hours, but the real economy barely moves yet.

events.title: Credit Growth Responds
events.description: Banks reprice loans, credit growth accelerates or slows, and businesses adjust investment plans.

events.title: Demand and Prices Actually Move
events.description: The change in credit and spending finally shows up in demand-pull pressure and, with a further lag, in the CPI print itself. This is why the RBI has to act on where inflation is heading, not where it is today.

cards.definition: Prices rise because aggregate spending power outruns the economy's productive capacity.
Prices rise because input costs (oil, food, wages) rise and are passed through, independent of demand.
Prices rise because the money supply grows faster than real output; the classic driver of hyperinflations.
How many times a unit of currency changes hands in the economy over a given period; a key variable in M x V = P x Q.
The painful combination of high inflation and weak growth (or high unemployment) at the same time, usually born from a cost-push shock.
Workers demand higher wages to keep up with inflation, employers raise prices to cover higher wages, and the cycle feeds itself.

body.title: The Hard Case
body.scenario: Global crude oil prices double after a geopolitical shock. Diesel and LPG prices in India rise sharply, and transport and packaged food costs follow within weeks. Bank credit growth, meanwhile, is flat, and the RBI has held its policy rate unchanged for a year.
body.prompt: Which engine is dominant here? Would an RBI rate hike actually bring this inflation down, and what is the tradeoff if the MPC hikes anyway?
body.modelAnswer: This is a textbook cost-push shock: credit is flat, so demand is not the driver, and the price surge is arriving through the input-cost channel (oil), not through household spending. A rate hike does very little to bring down the price of imported crude; it mainly slows an economy that was not overheating in the first place. This is the core stagflation dilemma covered in the 1970s chapter: the central bank can hike to defend its inflation target and credibility, but it pays for that with weaker growth, without actually fixing the underlying supply shock.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Home loan rates fall after a rate-cut cycle, NBFC credit growth crosses 15% year-on-year, and property prices across the NCR and Bengaluru jump sharply, while cement and steel costs stay roughly flat. Which engine best explains this?
options: Cost-push inflation from rising construction input costs
Monetary inflation from excess money supply growth alone
Demand-pull inflation from a credit-fuelled spending boom
A wage-price spiral in the construction sector
body.explanation: Input costs (cement, steel) are flat, so this is not cost-push. Credit growth and rate cuts are pulling demand forward faster than housing supply can respond, the classic demand-pull signature.

points: Demand-pull inflation comes from spending power outrunning supply; the classic signal is core inflation rising together with strong GDP growth.
Cost-push inflation comes from rising input costs, most often oil, food, or wages, and can hit even when credit growth and demand are flat.
Monetary inflation comes from the money supply outgrowing real output; the quantity theory identity M x V = P x Q shows why this must eventually push prices up.
Cost-push shocks are the hardest to fight with interest rates, because rate hikes slow demand without fixing the underlying supply problem, this is the root of stagflation.
Rate changes work with a lag, often 9 to 18 months before they show up fully in demand and prices, which is why the RBI acts on where inflation is heading, not just where it stands today.
